intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Three patients had heterozygous de novo variants in autosomal dominant genes: GABRA1, GABRB1, and ATP1A3.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a heterozygous de novo, likely pathogenic GABRB1 variant causing EIMFS, a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The DEE45 label is standard OMIM nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-45 (DEE45) is a severe neurologic disorder with onset of seizures in infancy. Reported patients have had infantile spasms (Epi4K Consortium et al., 2013; Janve et al., 2016) or epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures with severe to profound developmental impairment (Burgess et al., 2019). Janve et al. (2016) described the epileptic encephalopathies as a diverse group of severe childhood epilepsy syndromes with intractable seizures, neurodevelopmental delay and regression, resistance to treatment, and poor clinical outcomes.

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) sequenced the exomes of 264 probands with infantile spasms (149 patients) or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (115 patients) and their parents. Patients were enrolled through the Epilepsy Phenome/Genome Project. Patients with infantile spasms were required to have hypsarrhythmia on EEG. One proband carried a de novo mutation in GABRB1. Janve et al. (2016) stated that this patient had infantile spasms. They noted that the infantile spasms phenotype was severe in this patient and in a patient with a GABRB3 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Burgess et al. (2019) studied a cohort of 135 patients from 128 unrelated families with epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS). One patient (patient 63) had a de novo GABRB1 variant. Seizures in this patient began at 4 months of age, and the patient was 2 years old at the time of the study. The patient had focal seizures at onset, severe to profound developmental impairment, and hypotonia. EIMFS was defined in that study by focal seizures that migrated between the hemispheres, clinically and/or electrically, with onset before 6 months of age.

paragraphs.text: Janve et al. (2016) reported that the de novo GABRB1 mutation from the Epi4K study was a phe246-to-ser (F246S) substitution in a patient with infantile spasms. The patient was heterozygous for the mutation. F246 is an invariant residue across all GABA(A) receptor subunits and lies in transmembrane domain 1. The authors coexpressed mutant beta-1 subunits with alpha-1 and gamma-2L subunits in HEK293T cells. When only mutant beta-1 was expressed, peak GABA-evoked current density fell by 25%. In the heterozygous expression condition, current density was not affected. The mutation slowed current deactivation, and in single-channel recordings it increased mean open time about 3.75-fold and burst duration about 3.2-fold. Under the homozygous expression condition it increased holding currents about 5-fold, consistent with spontaneous channel openings. It also increased the open probability of spontaneous single-channel openings 4-fold. Surface levels of the mutant subunit were slightly but significantly reduced, without a change in total levels. Janve et al. (2016) concluded that all 5 de novo GABRB mutations studied impaired GABA(A) receptor function, and they suggested GABRB1 as a candidate human epilepsy gene.

paragraphs.text: In a cohort of 135 patients with EIMFS, Burgess et al. (2019) identified a heterozygous de novo ile247-to-thr (I247T) variant in GABRB1 (chr4:47405633T-C, GRCh37) in 1 patient (patient 63). The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing and was absent from the ExAC and gnomAD databases. PolyPhen classified it as benign and SIFT as deleterious. It was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria.

paragraphs.text: The Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) found a de novo GABRB1 mutation in 1 of 264 probands with infantile spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome who were studied by trio exome sequencing. In HEK293T cells, the mutation had little effect on peak GABA-evoked current, but it slowed deactivation and prolonged mean open time and burst duration. It also caused spontaneous channel openings, with increased holding currents and spontaneous open probability.

agent.process_note: I read the full texts of Epi4K Consortium et al. (2013) and Janve et al. (2016). For Burgess et al. (2019), I searched for GABRB1 and read the methods, results and phenotype/variant tables in full. Only the title of Lien et al. (2016) is available, so that paper is cited for its title alone. The Epi4K paper does not give the GABRB1 variant or the patient's phenotype in its text (these were in supplementary tables I don't have); the F246S name and the infantile spasms phenotype come from Janve et al. No nucleotide change was available for F246S. The patient's sex and further clinical details for the Burgess patient were not in the text. The Burgess phenotype table shows '1' under 'Sz-free' for GABRB1, but the main text does not list a GABRB1 patient among those who were seizure-free, so I left seizure outcome out. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the gene's MIM number and chromosomal location are left out of the intro.
